clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria caused by biallelic GCDH variants encoding glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a mitochondrial enzyme in the catabolism of lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan.
Macrocephaly, often present from birth or developing in infancy, is a characteristic and frequently overlooked early clue.

The cardinal risk is an acute encephalopathic (striatal) crisis, typically precipitated by an intercurrent febrile illness, fasting or the catabolic stress of vaccination or surgery during the vulnerable early-childhood window.
Striatal injury during a crisis produces an acquired, often irreversible dystonic-dyskinetic movement disorder with loss of motor milestones.
Neuroimaging characteristically shows frontotemporal atrophy with widened Sylvian fissures ('bat-wing' appearance), subdural collections and basal ganglia signal change.
Subdural haemorrhages and retinal haemorrhages can mimic non-accidental injury, a critical diagnostic pitfall.

Newborn screening (raised glutarylcarnitine) enables presymptomatic diagnosis, and emergency management with lysine restriction, carnitine supplementation and intensified energy provision during illness prevents striatal injury.
reference.pathophysiology: Glutaric aciduria type 1 is an autosomal recessive cerebral organic aciduria caused by deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, the mitochondrial flavoenzyme that catalyses the oxidative decarboxylation of glutaryl-CoA to crotonyl-CoA in the degradative pathway of the amino acids lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan. Enzyme deficiency leads to accumulation of glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid and glutarylcarnitine, and depletion of free carnitine. These dicarboxylic metabolites are thought to be neurotoxic, with excitotoxic and energy-impairing effects on the developing striatum, and they are poorly cleared across the blood-brain barrier so accumulate within the central nervous system. During episodes of increased catabolism, the surge in metabolite production overwhelms residual capacity and precipitates acute bilateral striatal necrosis, producing a dystonic movement disorder. A distinction is drawn between 'low excretor' and 'high excretor' biochemical phenotypes, which differ in urinary metabolite levels but not necessarily in neurological risk, so management is guided by clinical vulnerability rather than excretor status alone.

Non-accidental injury (given subdural and retinal haemorrhages)

Dystonic cerebral palsy of other aetiology
Other causes of acute encephalopathy in infancy
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised glutarylcarnitine) including newborn-screening result
Glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase enzyme activity assay where required
Brain MRI (frontotemporal atrophy, widened Sylvian fissures, subdural collections, basal ganglia change)
Plasma free and total carnitine measurement
Assessment for subdural and retinal haemorrhages with careful safeguarding differentiation
redFlags: Febrile illness, fasting or perioperative catabolic stress in a young child (crisis-precipitating window)
Acute loss of motor milestones or new dystonia/hypotonia during intercurrent illness
Progressive or disproportionate macrocephaly in infancy
Subdural and retinal haemorrhages raising both metabolic and safeguarding concern
Encephalopathy with basal ganglia signal change on imaging
reference.prognosis: With presymptomatic detection through newborn screening and rigorous emergency and maintenance management, most children can avoid striatal injury and achieve normal or near-normal neurological development. Once an encephalopathic crisis has caused striatal necrosis, the resulting dystonic movement disorder is usually permanent and disabling.
pitfalls: Misattributing subdural and retinal haemorrhages to non-accidental injury without considering GA1
Failing to institute aggressive emergency metabolic management during intercurrent illness, when striatal injury occurs
Assuming a 'low excretor' biochemical phenotype confers lower neurological risk and relaxing protection
Overlooking macrocephaly as an early sign before the first crisis
Delaying treatment until after a crisis, when neurological damage is largely irreversible
references: Standard textbook of inborn errors of metabolism

management: Start disease-specific dietary treatment with lysine restriction and arginine supplementation to reduce accumulation of the glutaryl-CoA-derived neurotoxic metabolites
Give L-carnitine supplementation to maintain free carnitine and enhance removal of glutarylcarnitine
Provide a written emergency regimen for febrile illness, vaccination or surgery, using generous glucose intake, transient protein reduction and intravenous glucose to avert a striatal crisis
Ensure prompt hospital admission during any catabolic stress in the first years of life for intensive intravenous glucose and carnitine with close neurological observation
Treat the acquired dystonic-dyskinetic movement disorder symptomatically, for example with baclofen or trihexyphenidyl, alongside physiotherapy and feeding support
Follow up growth, biochemistry and neurodevelopment within a specialist metabolic and dietetic service
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive GCDH inheritance, with newborn screening and presymptomatic testing of at-risk relatives
